Don DeLillo. Born in 1936, an American novelist celebrated for sprawling, densely plotted narratives that anatomize American paranoia, consumer culture, technology, and the specter of catastrophe. His novels—White Noise, Libra, Underworld—combine encyclopedic detail, tonal control, and a fascination with systems that have made him a defining postmodern voice in American literature. He is a master of systems themselves, observing how media, surveillance, and nuclear anxiety bind together the fabric of contemporary consciousness.

White Noise, published in 1985, follows a blended family navigating consumerism, media saturation, and existential dread. The novel treats television, supermarkets, and fear as the textual fabric of American life. Libra, from 1988, reimagines the Kennedy assassination through multiple perspectives and historical detail, treating history itself as an unstable text subject to reinterpretation and conspiracy. Underworld, published in 1997, spans Cold War America. It opens with the 1951 Giants-Dodgers baseball game, then spirals backward and forward through decades of nuclear anxiety, waste, and urban decay. DeLillo is a master of free indirect discourse and long accumulative paragraphs. His prose is baroque, digressive, cataloging the clutter of American material and informational excess. He treats major historical events as narrative events subject to textual instability and competing interpretations. His novels resist closure and moral clarity. They are formal experiments in representing contemporary consciousness under conditions of information overload and paranoia. Thomas Pynchon shares his postmodern preoccupation with systems and the erosion of individual agency, as does David Foster Wallace, with whom he shares an interest in media, consumption, and consciousness.
